narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimates a 77% chance you would not pass the bar exam on the first attempt, making the risk of admitting you too high. The most important factor in that decision was your class rank in the third year of law school. You ranked in the bottom decile—specifically the 1st decile—while admitted students typically rank around the 6th decile. This far-below-average standing strongly pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure, and it outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score actually helped you. Although your score of 36 is slightly below the typical admitted student’s average of 37.18, the model treated it as a point in your favor, nudging the prediction toward passing. That positive influence was the second strongest factor overall, but it was not enough to offset your class rank.

Your family income bracket also influenced the outcome, but to a smaller degree. Being from a middle-income background pushed slightly toward the failure side, especially when compared with the admitted pool, which is mostly upper-middle and high income. However, this factor carries far less weight than your third-year standing.

To improve your chances on reapplication, focus on raising your academic performance in your final year. Take a lighter course load if needed, seek tutoring or study groups, and aim to move yourself into a higher decile. Retaking the LSAT could also help, but your class rank is the single clearest signal to strengthen.
